A Confidence-Calibrated Triage Framework for Pneumonia Detection and Multi-Architecture Stability Analysis

Abstract — Pneumonia is one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, particularly among children under five years of age, and its timely detection from chest radiographs remains a critical clinical challenge. This research work presents an automated pneumonia detection pipeline using the publicly available Chest X-Ray Images (Pneumonia) dataset and a comparative study of five pre-trained deep learning architectures. Rather than developing a novel architectural design, this work studies the classification performance of DenseNet121, ResNet50, EfficientNet-B0, VGG16, and MobileNetV3-Large under identical training conditions. Beyond binary classification, a Confidence-Calibrated Triage System is proposed as the novel contribution, assigning one of three clinical priority levels — LOW RISK, UNCERTAIN, and HIGH RISK — based on model confidence with fully tunable thresholds. DenseNet121 achieved the best performance with 93.91% accuracy, 98.29% AUC-ROC, 98.21% sensitivity, and 86.75% specificity on the held-out test set.

Index Terms — Pneumonia Detection, Chest X-ray, Deep Learning, Transfer Learning, DenseNet121, Confidence Calibration, Clinical Triage, Grad-CAM, Class Imbalance, Medical Image Analysis

I. Introduction

Pneumonia accounts for approximately 15% of all deaths of children under five globally, making it the single largest infectious cause of child mortality worldwide. Clinical diagnosis primarily relies on chest radiograph interpretation — a task that demands significant radiologist expertise and is prone to inter-reader variability. In low-resource environments, an AI-assisted screening tool that is fast, accurate, and transparent could provide substantial clinical value.

The use of computer vision and deep learning has become more prevalent in analyzing chest X-rays for disease detection. However, in the evaluation of models using traditional approaches, there is an emphasis on accuracy and other performance measures but not on confidence communication. A model assigning 52% probability to PNEUMONIA and one assigning 97% produce the same output label, yet their clinical implications are entirely different.

This study addresses three research gaps: (1) Uncertainty Communication — most pneumonia detection research concentrates on reporting classification metrics without communicating prediction confidence; (2) Multi-Architecture Analysis — a systematic comparison of five architectures under identical conditions; and (3) Clinical Deployability — a three-level confidence output mapping directly to clinical priority queues.

II. Literature Review

Rajpurkar et al. developed CheXNet, a 121-layer DenseNet-based system trained on ChestX-ray14 for chest-radiograph disease detection [2]. The work demonstrated that deep learning could achieve strong performance and established DenseNet121 as the reference backbone for chest X-ray classification tasks.

CheXNeXt revealed high efficiency of deep learning models but also pointed to challenges in certain pathology identification, highlighting the persistent gap between benchmark accuracy and real clinical reliability [3].

Wang et al. concentrated on the highly skewed nature of class distribution in ChestX-ray14 and proposed adaptive sampling with representation learning [5]. This indicates that class skewness can have a substantial impact on the task of diagnosing diseases of the thorax.

Researchers studied the robustness of chest X-ray classification models to noise and variations in inputs, showing that conventional performance on the test set does not necessarily translate into robust performance [14]. This motivates the confidence calibration approach in this work.

III. Dataset Description

This research uses the Chest X-Ray Images (Pneumonia) dataset published by Kermany et al. (2018), hosted on Kaggle under CC BY 4.0. It contains 5,863 chest X-rays from paediatric patients aged 1–5 years from Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center, China. Labels were validated by two expert physicians and one third-party reviewer.

IV. Proposed Methodology

The proposed methodology builds and evaluates a pneumonia detection pipeline using five pre-trained CNN architectures under identical conditions, and extends the best-performing model with a confidence-calibrated triage system. Fig. 2 provides the full system pipeline.

Fig. 2. Full system pipeline: Data Layer, Model Layer, Training Layer, Output Layer.

Given an input chest X-ray X, the classifier provides the pneumonia probability as:

P₀ = fθ(X)     (1)

A. Baseline Classifier Architectures

Five pre-trained CNN architectures are evaluated. Each model's original ImageNet head is replaced with a custom binary head. DenseNet121 uses dense connectivity where each layer receives concatenated feature maps from all preceding layers:

xₗ = Hₗ([x₀, x₁, ..., xₗ₋₁])     (2)

ResNet50 uses residual connections H(x) = F(x) + x. EfficientNet-B0 uses compound scaling. VGG16 uses uniform 3×3 convolutions. MobileNetV3-Large uses depthwise separable convolutions with squeeze-and-excitation attention.

Fig. 3. DenseNet121 architecture with dense connectivity and custom classification head.

B. Image Preprocessing and Model Training

Images are resized to 224×224 and normalised using ImageNet statistics. Training augmentations include RandomCrop, RandomHorizontalFlip (p=0.5), RandomRotation (±10°), ColorJitter, and RandomAffine. The classifier is trained using weighted cross-entropy loss:

L_WCE = -(1/N) ∑ᵢ wᵉᵢ · log(p̂(yᵢ|xᵢ))     (3)

Weights: w_NORMAL = 1.945, w_PNEUMONIA = 0.673. Adam optimiser (lr=1×10⁻⁴), StepLR scheduler (step=7, γ=0.1), early stopping (patience=5).

Fig. 4. Loss function equations, Adam optimiser rule, StepLR schedule, and evaluation metrics.

Fig. 5. Detailed training pipeline with early stopping and best-model checkpointing flow.

C. Confidence-Calibrated Triage System

The triage system converts P(PNEUMONIA) into one of three clinical priority levels using tunable thresholds T_high and T_low:

HIGH RISK  if P₀ ≥ 0.80     (4)

LOW RISK   if P₀ ≤ 0.20     (5)

UNCERTAIN  otherwise        (6)

Fig. 6. Confidence-Calibrated Triage System: 3-level clinical decision with tunable thresholds.

D. Grad-CAM Interpretability

Grad-CAM produces spatial heatmaps highlighting discriminative image regions. Gradients are pooled over spatial dimensions to weight activation maps:

αᵏᶠ = (1/Z) ∑ᵢ∑ⴕ ∂yᶠ/∂Aᵏᵢⴕ     (7)

Lᶠ = ReLU(∑ᵏ αᵏᶠ · Aᵏ)              (8)

F. Discussion

DenseNet121 outperforms other architectures because dense connectivity allows every layer to access feature maps from all preceding layers, enabling simultaneous multi-scale feature reuse. For pneumonia detection where subtle textural consolidation patterns matter, this is a decisive advantage over ResNet's additive residuals or VGG16's sequential feature propagation.

VGG16 lags despite 138M parameters because it lacks skip connections. The model achieves 98.21% sensitivity at 86.75% specificity — a deliberate asymmetry that is clinically appropriate, since a missed pneumonia case can be fatal while a false alarm leads to further investigation rather than direct harm.

VI. Conclusion

This paper presented a comprehensive deep learning pipeline for pneumonia detection from chest X-rays, comparing five pre-trained CNN architectures under identical training conditions. DenseNet121 achieved the best performance with 93.91% accuracy, 98.29% AUC-ROC, 98.21% sensitivity, and 86.75% specificity.

The novel contribution is the Confidence-Calibrated Triage System, which transforms raw softmax probabilities into three clinical priority levels with fully tunable thresholds. By introducing an explicit UNCERTAIN output level, the system routes ambiguous cases to radiologist review rather than forcing potentially incorrect binary decisions — directly addressing the core safety requirement of AI in clinical medicine.
